data.title: Hong Kong Targets Unlicensed Crypto Businesses With New Rules, Jail Terms and Heavy Fines
data.description:
Hong Kong is preparing to extend its crypto regulatory framework beyond trading platforms, bringing businesses involved in digital asset dealing, investment advice, portfolio management and custody under closer supervision.

The proposed legislation would require these service providers to obtain licences or register with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), while introducing penalties for businesses that falsely claim to hold a licence or use regulated industry titles without authorisation.

Hong Kong Expands Crypto Licensing Rules Beyond Trading Platforms

The Hong Kong government gazetted the Virtual Asset Services Legislation (Amendment) Bill 2026 on 20 November, proposing amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance.

The bill would bring four additional virtual asset activities under the SFC's supervision, covering cryptocurrency dealing, advisory services, asset management and custody.

Hong Kong's virtual asset bill also reaches HKMA-regulated banks and stored value facility licensees. The government gazetted it on 20 Nov 2026 and says those firms would be required to be registered with the Securities and Futures Commission if they wish to provide any VA… pic.twitter.com/792hWBXnhM

— Romeo (@romeo_fardeen) November 21, 2026

Businesses providing these services in Hong Kong would need to obtain the appropriate licence or register with the regulator, subject to a fit-and-proper assessment and other regulatory requirements.

The proposal builds on the city's existing licensing framework for virtual asset trading platforms, extending oversight to other businesses handling customers' digital assets or providing investment-related services.

Christopher Hui, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury, said the framework follows the principle of "same activity, same risks, same regulation".

The government also said it had considered international anti-money laundering standards and existing investor protection requirements in Hong Kong's financial markets.

False Licence Claims Could Lead To Jail Time And Daily Fines

The bill introduces penalties targeting businesses and individuals who misrepresent their regulatory status.

According to CoinNess, citing Caixin, anyone claiming to be a licence applicant without having submitted an actual application could face up to two years in prison and a HK$400,000 fine upon conviction on indictment.

An additional HK$10,000 fine could apply for every day the offence continues.

🇭🇰 UPDATE: Hong Kong bill proposes up to 2 years in jail and HK400K(~51K) fine for falsely claiming to be a crypto licence applicant, plus HK$10K daily.

— CryptoMeter.io (@CryptoMeterIO) November 21, 2026

A separate provision targets businesses using titles associated with SFC-regulated virtual asset services without the necessary licence or registration.

These include cryptocurrency dealer, cryptocurrency adviser and virtual asset custodian.

Offenders could face a HK$100,000 fine, with a further HK$2,000 for each day the offence continues.

The provisions distinguish between falsely claiming to have applied for regulatory approval and using professional titles that suggest a business is authorised to provide regulated services.

The SFC already maintains separate public records for licensed trading platforms and operators with pending applications.

Some applicants benefit from a transitional arrangement that deemed them licensed from 1 June 2024 while their applications were under review.

However, the regulator can still reject their applications and require them to close their Hong Kong operations.

Banks And Crypto Custodians Face Additional Oversight

The proposed framework would also cover banks and licensed stored-value facility operators supervised by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA).

These institutions would need to register with the SFC if they intend to provide virtual asset services in Hong Kong.

Both the SFC and HKMA would receive powers to administer and oversee the expanded regulatory framework.

The custody requirements would apply to businesses safeguarding customers' crypto assets or controlling the private keys used to authorise transactions.

The HKMA had already issued guidance in May for banks planning to provide digital asset custody services.

Institutions were asked to consult the authority before launching such services, while existing providers were told to review their security arrangements.

The guidance covers private keys, recovery seeds and backup systems, as well as controls maintained by subsidiaries holding digital assets for customers.

It also applies when custody is provided independently or alongside the distribution of tokenised financial products.

Why Are Crypto Advisers And Asset Managers Getting Separate Licences?

The government has revised its approach to investment advice and portfolio management following industry feedback.

Earlier proposals considered placing both activities under the same licensing category as crypto dealing.

However, the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau and the SFC later developed separate categories for advisory and management services.

The distinction centres on who makes the investment decision.

Hong Kong’s crypto bill is no longer just a broker-and-custodian bill.

In December 2025, regulators dropped the idea of rolling advice and portfolio management into the dealer licence. Those became two separate tracks, modelled on the way Hong Kong already distinguishes… pic.twitter.com/LAGK7k3oKg

— Zest Research｜加密研究 (@zestsports_eth) November 23, 2026

Advisers recommending specific virtual assets to customers would fall under the proposed advisory regime, while asset managers exercising discretion over clients' portfolios would require authorisation under the management framework.

Automated services generating specific virtual asset investment recommendations could also fall within the advisory requirements.

However, general market information and software that filters factual data for customers conducting their own research would be treated differently.

For portfolio managers, the proposed rules draw on Hong Kong's existing framework for discretionary securities management.

Regulators have not proposed a minimum virtual asset allocation for determining whether a portfolio falls within the regime.

Managers overseeing portfolios containing both traditional securities and virtual assets could therefore require authorisation under both regulatory frameworks.

The consultations received 101 submissions on dealing and 93 on custody.

A separate consultation covering advice and management attracted 51 responses.

Most respondents supported separate licences for advisory and management activities, although some requested greater clarity on their scope and exemptions.

Hong Kong Lawmakers Will Review The Bill On 2 December

The legislation is scheduled for its first reading in the Legislative Council on 2 December 2026.

It must still pass through the legislative process before the proposed licensing requirements can take effect.

Hong Kong has published a bill that would extend crypto licensing to custody services.

Banks and stored value facility operators would also need to register with the SFC before offering virtual asset services.

The first reading is scheduled for December 2. Link in reply.

— CrispyBull (@CrispyBull) November 23, 2026

The expansion has also raised concerns about the impact on existing businesses.

In January, the Hong Kong Securities and Futures Professionals Association warned that introducing new licences without transitional arrangements could force businesses to suspend operations while their applications were reviewed.

The association called for a grace period of six to 12 months to give affected firms time to meet the new requirements.

However, the government's announcement did not specify whether such arrangements would be introduced.

The proposal follows other regulatory actions by the SFC.

On 18 November, the regulator added Hyperliquid to its list of suspicious virtual asset trading platforms, stating that the platform lacked an SFC licence and might have marketed its services to Hong Kong residents.

The proposed legislation would further expand the city's oversight of the digital asset industry, although its final requirements will depend on the legislative process and any amendments made before approval.

data.title: The Nasdaq wiped out a year's worth of gains in a single day. How should we interpret the fund flows during this sharp decline?
data.description:
Produced by: Block Analytics × Merkle 3s Capital

On November 20, 2026, the Nasdaq fell 5.28% in a single day, wiping out all gains since the beginning of 2026.

A global fund manager survey released in the same month (survey period November 6-12, 2026) showed that the proportion of cash held by fund managers dropped from 3.9% to 3.6%, with almost no one hoarding money.

As of the week ending November 18, global equity funds saw a net inflow of $59.23 billion. Prices are fleeing, but money isn't. Which set of figures should we believe? Fund managers are selling AI, not stocks. First, let's explain what this survey is. FMS is a monthly questionnaire conducted by Bank of America with global fund managers, asking them what they hold, what they fear, and how they want companies to spend money. In the November survey, 169 fund managers answered the global questions, managing a total of approximately $461 billion.

Bank of America FMS Technology Reduction History Chart

The most striking change is the technology portfolio. Net overweighting of technology stocks fell from 37% in October to 12%, a 25 percentage point decrease in one month, the largest monthly drop since June 2006.

But the money wasn't taken home. The cash ratio fell from 3.9% in October to 3.6%, the lowest since August.

Overall, stocks remain net overweight by 41%, with only about 3% expecting a recession. A 25% reduction in tech holdings in a month resulted in cash holdings dropping to 3.6%. Money didn't leave the market, it just left AI! Why specifically AI? Three other sets of readings from the survey provide the answer. Tail risk refers to events with low probability but the greatest potential damage: 34% chose an AI bubble, and 31% chose credit events involving AI cloud vendors, totaling 65%. In the October survey, these two items combined accounted for only 34%. Crowded trading refers to positions where everyone is crowding onto the same side, narrowing the exit points: Long positions in global semiconductors still rank first, accounting for 39%. The record in July was 82%, indicating that the crowding is receding, but not completely. Cash usage: Only 16% want companies to spend more on capex, i.e., capital expenditures for buying chips and building data centers, the lowest since May 2020. 52% expect major companies to announce spending cuts within six months, and a net 38% of respondents believe that companies are over-investing, a record for this survey. Fund managers aren't most concerned about AI demand, but rather the cost of AI. Orders are still rising; they're asking who will pay and how much they need to borrow. Fund managers aren't afraid of a lack of demand for AI; they're afraid of nobody paying the bills for AI! Looking at only one survey can lead to a biased view. We break down fund flows into five tables: Interest Rate Table: The price of money, including interest rates, the US dollar, and expectations of interest rate hikes. Liquidity Table: The quantity of money, including net liquidity, reverse repos, and bank reserves. Position Table: How fund managers allocate their portfolios, as shown in the questionnaire above. Pipeline Table: The money investors actually subscribe to and redeem from the fund. Credit Table: The rates offered to borrowers in the bond market. Each table has two states. "On" indicates a risk warning; "Release" indicates a release signal, meaning that most investors have exited, and the downward trend can then stop. Bank of America also has a cash rule: a cash level below 4.0% is a contrarian warning, while a level above 5.0% presents a contrarian opportunity. Reportedly, this warning has been triggered 12 times since 2011, with global stocks subsequently falling by an average of about 2.4% in the following month. The magnitude is small; it's more like a thermometer than an alarm clock. Its strategy team set an even closer threshold for the November survey on November 13th: cash levels must rise above 4.2%, while "prosperity" expectations (the percentage of people who believe future growth and inflation are above trend) must fall significantly for panic to be considered sufficient and sentiment to cease being a drag. The actual result was that cash fell to 3.6%, and "prosperity" expectations only decreased from 47% to 41%. Neither condition was met. Let me state my conclusion first: Of the five tables, the interest rate table and the position table are already lit up, the credit table and the liquidity table are half lit up, and the pipeline table is not lit up yet; before cash rises above 4.2%, this is more like a stampede caused by a change of seats, not a release of control. The interest rate table is lit first: money is more expensive, and the buffer is gone. Let's look at the price of money first. On November 17, the 10-year US Treasury yield was 5.10%, and the US dollar index closed at 103.87 on November 18, the highest since April 2025. The more expensive the US dollar, the higher the cost for global funds to hold assets outside the US. The expectation of interest rate hikes is more direct. On November 17, the 2-year US Treasury yield was 4.80%, which is the most sensitive point to interest rate hike expectations. As of November 20, the federal funds rate was between 3.75% and 4.00%, having already been raised once in September. At the close of trading on November 19, interest rate futures implied a probability of another rate hike in December of approximately 96%. The minutes of the October policy meeting listed "whether AI-related investments can continue" and "how financing conditions will evolve" as items to be assessed. AI financing has been added to the central bank's watch list. Cash assets can obtain approximately 3.9% interest, while 10-year US Treasury bonds offer 5.1%. The threshold for AI companies to prove their returns exceed this line has been raised. The interest rate table is flashing a warning sign. The same survey also asked: At what 10-year yield would you be willing to switch from stocks to bonds? The weighted answer was 5.8%, about 70 basis points higher than the approximately 5.1% reported in the initial survey. The closer to this line, the less attractive stocks become. Bank of America's strategy team also outlined the conditions for an interest rate shift on November 13th: a 10-year yield falling below 4.5%, oil prices falling below $70 per barrel, and a weakening dollar. As of November 20th, none of these conditions had been met, and the dollar was still appreciating. The higher the return on holding cash, the higher the barrier to entry for holding AI! Let's look at the liquidity table. Net liquidity is a proxy indicator: the Fed's total assets minus the money the Treasury holds at the Fed, minus reverse repos. According to our calculations, it has fluctuated between approximately $5.75 trillion and $5.87 trillion since August. The liquidity hasn't decreased. The problem lies in the buffer. Reverse repos are a tool used by money market funds to lend idle funds to the Fed in the short term, and in the past, they served as a buffer for the market. It was approximately $2.55 trillion on December 30, 2022, but by November 18, 2026, it had dwindled to only $331 million, almost zero. Bank reserves are the money banks hold with the Federal Reserve. As of the week ending November 11, they totaled approximately $2.961 trillion, not far from the low of $2.894 trillion in the week ending October 28. The buffer is gone; the next time funding demand increases, the shock will fall more directly on reserves. Therefore, the water level gauge is only half-lit: the total amount hasn't tightened, but the buffer has been used up. The water in the pool hasn't decreased, but the shock-absorbing buffer is gone! The questionnaire shows that while investors are reducing their holdings, their wallets are still buying, and bonds are already being quoted. Fund subscriptions and redemptions are the net amount after deducting redeemed shares from the amount subscribed. The questionnaire records ideas, while subscriptions and redemptions record real money. The two sets of weekly statistics have different statistical methods, so let's look at them separately: A set of global fund flow statistics shows that in the week ending November 11, global equity funds saw a net inflow of $98.3 billion, the largest since June. Another data provider shows that, as of the week ending November 18, global equity funds saw net inflows of $59.23 billion, the largest weekly inflow since mid-June. In the same week, technology funds saw net inflows of $12.3 billion, while bond funds experienced net outflows for the second consecutive week, amounting to $3.2 billion. While fund managers were cutting tech investments in surveys, their wallets were still flowing into the stock market. Inflows continued into the week ending November 18; the worst days of decline, November 19 and 20, are not included in this data. Cracks first appear in the narrowest parts of the pipe. Secondary market tracking shows that semiconductor ETFs turned to net outflows in the week ending November 19, with varying amounts across different ETFs; we're only looking at the direction. Another sentiment indicator from Bank of America shows that equity fund flows were at the 96th percentile historically at the November survey point. This means that money is flowing into the stock market faster than at most times in history. The main channels are still flowing in, but the smaller channels are starting to leak. The indicator hasn't lit up yet. The survey says to run, wallets say to buy, and bonds have already set prices! The credit table looks at the interest rate spread, which is the extra interest borrowers pay compared to government bonds. The wider the spread, the more worried the market is about borrowers defaulting. The spread for broad-based junk bonds was 3.43 percentage points on November 17th, compared to 3.20% on November 12th, widening by about 23 basis points in five trading days. The level remains narrow, indicating no systemic panic. However, individual AI borrowers are a different story. Neocloud, an emerging AI cloud company that expands its computing power through debt financing, had a worst-case yield of approximately 15.2% (secondary market interpretation) on November 18th for its bonds maturing in 2030; this falls within the range for distressed bonds. Putting the two figures together: the broad-based spread is just over 3%, while the individual spread has exceeded 10 percentage points. The entire junk bond market is still borrowing normally, except for one AI company that is expanding production by borrowing money, which has seen its price increased. In the same survey, 38% of fund managers believe that the next systemic credit event is most likely to come from AI cloud vendor bonds. For highly leveraged companies, bad news often appears first in bonds, then in stock prices. The creditworthiness statement is half-revealed. Broad-based spreads are still narrow, but individual spreads have already widened. The gap itself is a signal! The drop on November 20th, following the order of the lights. Arrange the readings of each meter by time and compare them with the stock price: November 6th to 12th: Bank of America FMS survey conducted. November 13th: Bank of America strategy team gives a cash threshold of 4.2%. November 17: Survey results released, position tables lit up. On the same day, the 10-year US Treasury yield was 5.10%, and the spread between broad-based junk bonds was 3.43 percentage points. November 18: Yields on bonds issued by single-name AI borrowers were approximately 15.2%, and the US dollar index was 103.87. November 19: Anthropic listed on Nasdaq. The initial offering was $81.3 billion, surpassing SpaceX's approximately $75 billion offering; ranking second in history in terms of valuation. The offering price was $83, opening at $111.50, rising as much as 34%, before closing at $97.17, a 17.1% increase. On the same day, the Nasdaq fell 2.25%, and the S&P 500 and Dow Jones also fell by more than 2%. On November 20th: Anthropic closed at $88.30, down 9.13%, with an intraday low of $83.05, just 5 cents away from the offering price. The new shares were caught, but the AI ​​trading failed! The subscription frenzy didn't translate into enthusiasm for AI blockchain in the secondary market. Half of the opening gains were wiped out in a single day, and the next day it almost returned to its offering price. The main focus on November 20th was Nvidia. It closed at $125.53, a 14.01% drop in a single day. This marked seven consecutive days of decline on the daily chart and seven consecutive weeks of decline, the longest weekly losing streak since July 2008. Its market capitalization evaporated by approximately $1.16 trillion in seven trading days. Based on earnings over the past twelve months (TTM), its price-to-earnings ratio is now only about 13.5. Its performance hasn't broken down. The company reported quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion on November 17, a 103% year-over-year increase. Demand was confirmed by the financial report, yet the stock price still fell. This is exactly what the position table was referring to: the market isn't afraid of demand, it's afraid of the bills. That afternoon, media outlets, citing sources familiar with the matter, reported that regulators were investigating the company's accounting practices. Neither the company nor the regulators commented. An investigation does not equate to illegality. The indices followed suit. The Nasdaq fell 5.28%, closing at 22,617.73 points, turning its gains since 2026 negative. The S&P 500 fell 3.70%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.93%, both entering correction territory, meaning they had fallen more than 10% from their highs. The Nasdaq 100 fell as much as 20% from its intraday high, and the VIX fear index rose above 30 during the session. Another large investment bank's trading desk estimated that trend-following funds had sold approximately $57 billion worth of stocks in the month ending November 20. Using the same model, if the index traded sideways, they would sell another $65.8 billion; if it continued to fall, they would sell up to another $80.6 billion. This is a model estimate, not actual trading data, but it explains why the decline accelerated itself. After reviewing the answers, there are two layers of conclusion. First, the indicator light came on first: the interest rate table and position table had already given signals around November 17, but the stock price only reflected these signals on November 20. Second, the indicator light only explains "why it collapsed so easily," not "when it collapsed." Prices are already panicking, but cash isn't! The same set of tables, four categories of AI stocks each have their own set to watch. How can these five tables be applied to specific stocks? We divide AI stocks into four groups based on the flow of funds, and we look at one main table for each group first.

Infographic of Four Types of AI Stocks

Those who borrow moneyrely on external financing for capacity expansion. Once the interest rate spread falls below 1,000 basis points, capacity expansion will run out of funds, so first look at the credit report. NBIS's financial report illustrates this point: operating cash flow in the third quarter was approximately negative $273 million, and accounts receivable jumped by approximately $3.76 billion in the first quarter. Revenue is recorded on the books first, but the cash has not yet been received.

Those who collect moneyrevenue comes from cloud vendors' capex. ANET has almost no debt and isn't afraid of interest rate spreads; its only concern is having its clients' budgets cut. Two things need to be examined: the cash usage in the questionnaire and the creation and redemption of semiconductor ETFs. When an ETF is redeemed, its constituent stocks are sold off directly according to their weighting. Here's a detail: the largest weighting of the two mainstream semiconductor ETFs is different: one is AMD, about 10.5%; the other is NVDA, about 17.5%. Even with "semiconductor ETF outflows," the stocks affected are different. The ones paying the price are the four major cloud providers. Shareholders want them to first improve their balance sheets and spend less money, while the passive inflows into broad-based index funds are providing a safety net. This group needs to be analyzed separately: According to reports, only one company still has positive free cash flow, one slightly lowered its 2026 capex forecast, and another said it would significantly increase in 2027. The company receiving US dollars is TSMC. A strong US dollar affects cross-border funds; it has about 10% weighting in one semiconductor ETF. The capex guidance is two-sided. Major companies announcing cost cuts are positive for cash flow, improving cash flow; negative for receiving cash, leading to fewer orders. The same news can cause the two groups of stocks to move in opposite directions. Even among AI stocks, some are afraid of interest rates, some are afraid of interest rate spreads, and some are afraid of shareholders! These five tables can also go wrong. Let's start with where they might go wrong. First: Sentiment is the echo of market movements. A study covering decades of data examined dozens of factors predicting the stock market, most of which failed out of the sample. Questionnaire readings are highly correlated with past gains and losses, but have weak predictive power for future short-term returns. Optimism only arises when prices rise, and pessimism only arises when prices fall. Position tables are only used to measure crowding levels, not for market timing. Second point: Sentiment indicators actually measure interest rate cycles. Another study found that about 63% of the fluctuations in mainstream sentiment indices can be explained by macroeconomic and interest rate variables. Stripped of this, pure sentiment has almost no predictive power. This is precisely why interest rates are ranked first. When the 10-year rate is 5.10% and the probability of a rate hike is about 96%, simply looking at "tech positions being sold off at record lows" and entering the market contrarily can easily misjudge the interest rate cycle as excessive sentiment. Third point: Market structure has changed, old measures will become inaccurate. As passive funds grow larger, active funds naturally need to hold less cash, potentially triggering false alarms due to cash flow restrictions. This survey only interviewed approximately 170 to 190 active fund managers, obscuring passive funds, corporate buybacks, and quantitative funds. A counterexample is in 2026: According to reports, the Bank of America sentiment indicator mentioned earlier consistently showed a negative trend from May 26th to mid-October, nearly five months, while the S&P 500 actually rose by about 3% during the same period. Therefore, all five financial statements should be examined together. The pipeline statement fills in the gaps in the data that the survey didn't cover. After narrowing, the most reliable data in the research is the credit statement, especially for highly leveraged companies. This is also why single-name credit is listed separately in the subsequent release criteria. Sentiment indicators are often an echo of market movements, not the cause of the market! How to identify bottoming signals? A single signal is insufficient to confirm a bottom. We tend to wait for at least two independent dimensions to improve simultaneously. The thresholds in the chart are observation lines, not trading instructions. As of the closing on November 20th, none of the indicators in the chart reached the release reading.

Five-Table Stop-Loss Signal Information Chart

There are roughly two types of letting go:

  • Surrender Style: A large net outflow occurs in the pipeline table, cash jumps by 4.2% in the December survey, and both the pipeline table and the position table reverse direction.

    **Loosening Stance:** The 10-year yield has fallen back below 4.5%, the US dollar has retreated from its high, and the yield on individual AI bonds has fallen significantly, indicating a shift in both the interest rate and credit tables. If it's just an index rebound with no change in cash or subscriptions/redemptions, then it's still a change of position, not a complete loosening of grip. Conversely, if subscriptions/redemptions turn into large outflows, but cash remains below 4%, it indicates that money is flowing out, positions haven't been cleared, and the downtrend may not be over. Data in this article is as of the closing price on November 20, 2026.

    Not waiting for one light, but for several lights to light up together! The price has already told you it's scared. Cash and redemption haven't even started yet.

    Conclusion:Next time, check the table first!

data.description:
Sky Protocol processed more than $2 billion in USDS stablecoin redemptions on Thursday, coinciding with a CoinDesk investigation linking $518 million in transactions through its infrastructure to wallets associated with hackers, sanctioned entities and other illicit actors.

Circulating supply of Sky's USDS stablecoin dropped to about $3.16 billion from $5.24 billion in a day, per DefiLlama, the same day as a Nov. 19 report on illicit-linked flows through Sky. Sky said its Peg Stability Module "has processed over $968 billion in volume since inception" and that the alleged figures would be roughly 0.03% of that. https://t.co/0nqbzXFAqP

— Laura Shin (@laurashin) November 20, 2026

The withdrawals saw users exchange Sky's USDS stablecoin for Circle's USDC through its Peg Stability Module (PSM), which allows holders to swap the tokens at a fixed rate. Despite the scale of the redemptions, Sky maintained that USDS held its $1 peg throughout the withdrawals, while pushing back against the investigation's findings.

The development places Sky under increased scrutiny as the protocol faces questions over its exposure to illicit crypto transactions and the resilience of its stablecoin infrastructure.

Sky Processes $2 Billion in USDS Redemptions as Scrutiny Intensifies

Sky said on Friday that the amount of USDC held in its PSM never fell below $800 million during the withdrawals and had climbed back above $1.1 billion. The protocol also maintained that its PSM continued to facilitate USDS-to-USDC exchanges at a 1:1 rate throughout the redemption wave.

We’re aware of the recent CoinDesk report on activity involving the Sky Protocol Peg Stability Module (PSM), predominantly via third-party permissionless platforms. Reports like this are taken seriously across the Sky Ecosystem. For scale: the PSM has processed over $968 billion in volume since inception. The alleged figures would represent roughly 0.03% of that. The PSM is open, onchain infrastructure that supports the USDS and DAI peg by swapping stablecoins 1:1. Within Sky Ecosystem, associated Sky Agent front ends such as @sparkfinance, @grovedotfinance, @SkyMoney and @OseroHQ block users in sanctioned jurisdictions by screening and blocking flagged wallets. Participants across the Sky Ecosystem will continue doing their part alongside the rest of DeFi.

— Sky (@SkyEcosystem) November 19, 2026

However, the withdrawals coincided with concerns raised by CoinDesk's investigation that Circle could freeze USDC held by Sky, potentially making it more difficult for users to redeem their stablecoins.

The investigation, published on Nov. 19, examined research by blockchain analytics firm Inca Digital, which identified $518 million in transactions involving wallets linked to hackers, sanctioned entities and other threat actors over five years. Around $101.9 million of the flagged activity was reportedly associated with North Korean actors, including wallets connected to the February 2025 Bybit hack.

EXCLUSIVE: North Korean hackers and other illicit actors routed $$518M through Sky’s Peg Stability Module, converting freezable $$USDC into unfreezable $$DAI and $$USDS, with $101.9M directly linked to wallets including those behind the Bybit hack, per Inca Digital. @sndr_krisztian reports.

— CoinDesk (@CoinDesk) November 19, 2026

The report also raised questions about the potential exposure of Sky's infrastructure to illicit activity, putting additional scrutiny on the protocol as billions of dollars in USDS redemptions were processed.

Sky Pushes Back Against $518M Illicit Transaction Findings

Sky challenged the investigation's findings, pointing to an assessment by Block Analitica, a risk adviser to the Sky ecosystem, which disputed several aspects of the report.

Block Analitica argued that the $518 million in flagged transactions represented less than 0.06% of the more than $960 billion processed through Sky's Peg Stability Modules. The firm also noted that approximately two-thirds of the identified activity occurred between 2021 and mid-2024, before Sky introduced its newer LitePSM system.
